questions.stem: In the Brønsted-Lowry model, what is an acid?
options: A compound or ion that donates protons
A compound or ion that accepts protons
A compound or ion that donates electrons
A compound that releases hydroxide ions
questions.explanation: Brønsted-Lowry acids donate H⁺ ions (protons) and bases accept them. Releasing hydroxide ions describes an older, narrower definition of a base.

questions.stem: Hydrogen chloride reacts with water: HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻. Which species acts as a base?
questions.explanation: Water accepts a proton from HCl to become H₃O⁺, so water is the base. HCl donates the proton, so it is the acid.

questions.stem: Which equation shows ammonia acting as a base in water?
questions.explanation: Ammonia accepts a proton from water, forming NH₄⁺ and leaving OH⁻. In the second and third equations the nitrogen species donates a proton, so it acts as an acid.

questions.stem: What is the conjugate base of the hydrogensulfate ion, HSO₄⁻?
questions.explanation: A conjugate base is what remains when an acid loses one proton. HSO₄⁻ minus H⁺ gives SO₄²⁻. H₂SO₄ is its conjugate acid.

questions.stem: What is the conjugate acid of the hydrogenphosphate ion, HPO₄²⁻?
questions.explanation: A conjugate acid has one more proton: HPO₄²⁻ plus H⁺ gives H₂PO₄⁻, and adding a positive charge changes 2− to 1−. PO₄³⁻ is its conjugate base.

questions.stem: Ethanoic acid reacts with ammonia: CH₃COOH + NH₃ → CH₃COO⁻ + NH₄⁺. Which are the conjugate acid-base pairs?
options: CH₃COO⁻ and NH₃; CH₃COOH and NH₄⁺
CH₃COOH and CH₃COO⁻; NH₄⁺ and NH₃
CH₃COOH and NH₃; CH₃COO⁻ and NH₄⁺
CH₃COOH and NH₄⁺; NH₃ and CH₃COO⁻
questions.explanation: Each conjugate pair differs by one proton. CH₃COOH loses a proton to become CH₃COO⁻, and NH₃ gains one to become NH₄⁺. The acid and base on the same side of the equation are not a conjugate pair.

questions.stem: In which reaction does water act as an acid?
questions.explanation: Water donates a proton to carbonate, forming OH⁻, so it acts as an acid. In the other reactions water accepts a proton and forms H₃O⁺, acting as a base.

questions.stem: What are acid-base indicators?
options: Salts that dissolve only in acidic solutions and give coloured precipitates
Metal ions whose colour depends on the temperature of the solution
Weak acids or bases whose acidic form has a different colour from their basic form
Strong acids that change colour when they are completely neutralised
questions.explanation: An indicator exists as an acidic form and its conjugate base. Changing the H⁺ concentration shifts the balance between the two forms, which have different colours.

questions.stem: An indicator is a weak acid: HIn (yellow) ⇌ H⁺ + In⁻ (blue). What colour is it in a strongly acidic solution, and why?
options: Blue, because acids remove protons from the indicator molecules
Yellow, because a high H⁺ concentration keeps most of it as HIn
Blue, because a high H⁺ concentration converts most of it to In⁻
Yellow, because a high H⁺ concentration removes all of the HIn
questions.explanation: Excess H⁺ ions combine with In⁻, so the indicator is mostly in its acidic form, HIn, which is yellow. In basic solution H⁺ is removed and the blue In⁻ form dominates.

questions.stem: Ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, contains four hydrogen atoms. Why is it classified as monoprotic?
options: Only one of its four hydrogen atoms is present as an H⁺ ion in the pure acid
It is a weak acid, and all weak acids donate only one proton
Only the hydrogen bonded to oxygen in the -COOH group can be donated
The three hydrogens of the CH₃ group are donated together as one unit
questions.explanation: The O-H hydrogen of the carboxyl group is polar enough to be donated; C-H hydrogens are not. Pure ethanoic acid is molecular, and weak acids such as carbonic acid can be polyprotic.

questions.stem: Ethanedioic acid has the structural formula HOOC-COOH. How is it classified?
questions.explanation: Each of the two -COOH groups has one O-H hydrogen that can be donated, so the acid can donate two protons per molecule. It has no other ionisable hydrogens.

questions.stem: In the structural formula of sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄, how are the atoms arranged?
options: A chain of O atoms joins the S atom, with an H atom at each end
A central S is bonded to two O atoms by double bonds and to two OH groups
A central S is bonded to four O atoms, with both H atoms bonded to the S
A central O is bonded to the S atom and to both H atoms by single bonds
questions.explanation: Sulfuric acid has two S=O bonds and two S-O-H groups around sulfur, which has an expanded octet. Both acidic hydrogens are bonded to oxygen, which is why it is diprotic.

questions.stem: Phosphoric acid, H₃PO₄, is triprotic. Which feature of its structural formula explains this?
options: All three H atoms are in O-H groups bonded to the central P atom
All three H atoms are bonded directly to the central P atom
The P atom has three lone pairs that can each accept a proton
It has three P=O double bonds that each release one H⁺ ion
questions.explanation: H₃PO₄ has one P=O bond and three P-O-H groups. Each polar O-H hydrogen can be donated, so it can lose three protons in turn.

questions.stem: Which equation shows sulfur trioxide reacting with water?
questions.explanation: Non-metal oxides are acidic and form oxyacids with water. SO₃ forms sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄; it is SO₂ that forms sulfurous acid, H₂SO₃.

questions.stem: Which is the balanced equation for tetraphosphorus decoxide reacting with water?
questions.explanation: Four H₃PO₄ contain 12 H and 16 O. Six H₂O supply the 12 H, and 10 + 6 = 16 O balances, so P₄O₁₀ + 6H₂O → 4H₃PO₄.

questions.stem: Which oxide forms a basic solution when added to water?
questions.explanation: Metal oxides are commonly basic: K₂O + H₂O → 2KOH. Sulfur dioxide, carbon dioxide and phosphorus oxides are non-metal oxides that form acidic solutions.

questions.stem: Quicklime, calcium oxide, is added to water. Which equation shows the reaction?
questions.explanation: Calcium oxide is a basic metal oxide and forms calcium hydroxide with water. The oxide ion accepts a proton from water, forming two hydroxide ions.

questions.stem: Which statement about neutralisation reactions is correct?
options: They release no energy, as the products are neutral
They are exothermic only when a carbonate is used
They are exothermic, so the temperature of the mixture rises
They are endothermic, so the temperature of the mixture falls
questions.explanation: The reaction H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O releases energy, so mixing an acid and a base warms the solution. This is true for neutralising hydroxides and oxides as well as carbonates.

questions.stem: Which is the ionic equation for hydrochloric acid reacting with sodium hydrogencarbonate solution?
questions.explanation: One H⁺ reacts with each HCO₃⁻ to give water and carbon dioxide, which bubbles off. Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are spectator ions and stay in solution; sodium chloride is soluble.

questions.stem: Sulfuric acid reacts with magnesium oxide. What are the products?
questions.explanation: An acid and a metal oxide give a salt and water. Hydrogen is produced when an acid reacts with a metal, not its oxide, and sulfate is SO₄²⁻, not sulfide.

questions.stem: Black copper(II) oxide powder dissolves in nitric acid to give a blue solution. Which is the ionic equation?
questions.explanation: CuO is an insoluble solid, so it is written in full. Its oxide ions take two protons to form water, releasing Cu²⁺ ions, which are blue. Nitrate ions are spectators.

questions.stem: Marble chips, CaCO₃, react with hydrochloric acid. Which is the ionic equation?
questions.explanation: Calcium carbonate is insoluble, so it appears as a solid, not as free CO₃²⁻ ions. It reacts with two H⁺ ions to give Ca²⁺, water and carbon dioxide; Cl⁻ is a spectator.

questions.stem: Which is the balanced full equation for sulfuric acid reacting with potassium hydrogencarbonate?
questions.explanation: Two KHCO₃ are needed for the two potassium ions in K₂SO₄, and each HCO₃⁻ gives one H₂O and one CO₂. The second equation is unbalanced in potassium.

questions.stem: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. What volume of 0.100 mol L⁻¹ hydrochloric acid neutralises 25.0 mL of 0.120 mol L⁻¹ sodium hydroxide?
20.0 mL of 0.150 mol L⁻¹ sulfuric acid is neutralised by 0.250 mol L⁻¹ sodium hydroxide: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. What volume of NaOH is needed?
questions.explanation: n(H₂SO₄) = 0.150 × 0.0200 = 3.00 × 10⁻³ mol, so n(NaOH) = 6.00 × 10⁻³ mol. V = 6.00 × 10⁻³ / 0.250 = 0.0240 L = 24.0 mL. Ignoring the 1 : 2 ratio gives 12.0 mL.

questions.stem: NaHCO₃ + HCl → NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. Use Na = 22.99, H = 1.008, C = 12.01, O = 16.00. What mass of sodium hydrogencarbonate neutralises a spill of 50.0 mL of 1.00 mol L⁻¹ hydrochloric acid?
questions.explanation: n(HCl) = 1.00 × 0.0500 = 0.0500 mol, which reacts 1 : 1 with NaHCO₃ (84.01 g mol⁻¹). m = 0.0500 × 84.01 = 4.20 g. 0.0500 is the amount in moles, not grams.

questions.stem: An antacid tablet of calcium carbonate exactly neutralises 0.0200 mol of stomach acid: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂. Use Ca = 40.08, C = 12.01, O = 16.00. What mass of CaCO₃ did it contain?
questions.explanation: Two moles of HCl react with one mole of CaCO₃, so n(CaCO₃) = 0.0100 mol and m = 0.0100 × 100.09 = 1.00 g. Using a 1 : 1 ratio gives 2.00 g.

questions.stem: What makes an acid a strong acid?
options: It ionises completely in aqueous solution
It is present at a high concentration
It can donate more than one proton
It reacts with metals to give hydrogen
questions.explanation: Strength describes the degree of ionisation: a strong acid such as HCl donates essentially all its protons to water. Concentration is how much acid is dissolved per litre, which is a separate idea.

questions.stem: Solutions of 0.10 mol L⁻¹ hydrochloric acid and 0.10 mol L⁻¹ ethanoic acid are compared. Why does the hydrochloric acid conduct electricity better and have a lower pH?
options: Ethanoic acid molecules are larger, so they carry the current more slowly
HCl ionises completely, but only a small fraction of ethanoic acid molecules ionise
HCl is more concentrated, so it contains more acid molecules in each litre
Ethanoic acid is diprotic, so its protons are shared and fewer ions form
questions.explanation: Both solutions have the same concentration of acid. HCl is a strong acid, so its solution has far more H⁺ and other ions than the weak ethanoic acid, which is mostly un-ionised.

questions.stem: Which description fits 6 mol L⁻¹ ethanoic acid?
options: A dilute solution of a strong acid
A concentrated solution of a weak acid
A dilute solution of a weak acid
A concentrated solution of a strong acid
questions.explanation: A lot of acid is dissolved per litre, so it is concentrated, but ethanoic acid only partly ionises, so it is weak. Strength and concentration are independent of each other.

questions.stem: Pure ethanoic acid does not conduct electricity, but its solution in water does. Why?
options: In water some molecules ionise, forming mobile H₃O⁺ and CH₃COO⁻ ions
Water molecules carry the current, and the pure acid has no water in it
The pure acid is a solid at room temperature, so its ions cannot move
In water the acid releases free electrons that carry the current
questions.explanation: Pure ethanoic acid is molecular, with no ions. In water a small fraction of molecules donate protons to water, and the resulting ions can carry charge. Pure ethanoic acid is a liquid at room temperature.

questions.stem: What is the pH of hydrochloric acid with [H⁺] = 0.010 mol L⁻¹?
questions.explanation: pH = −log[H⁺] = −log(1.0 × 10⁻²) = 2. A pH of 12 would be basic.

questions.stem: A solution has a pH of 3.5. What is its hydrogen ion concentration?
questions.explanation: Rearranging pH = −log[H⁺] gives [H⁺] = 10 to the power −pH, so [H⁺] = 10 to the power −3.5 = 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹. A pH between 3 and 4 must give a value between 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻³.

questions.stem: Lemon juice has a pH of 2 and tomato juice a pH of 4. How do their hydrogen ion concentrations compare?
options: Lemon juice has 100 times the [H⁺] of tomato juice
Lemon juice has twice the [H⁺] of tomato juice
Tomato juice has twice the [H⁺] of lemon juice
Lemon juice has 20 times the [H⁺] of tomato juice
questions.explanation: pH is a logarithmic scale: each unit is a factor of 10 in [H⁺]. A difference of 2 units is 10 × 10 = 100 times, with the lower pH more acidic.

questions.stem: 10.0 mL of 0.100 mol L⁻¹ hydrochloric acid is diluted with water to 1.00 L. What is the pH of the diluted solution?
questions.explanation: n(H⁺) = 0.100 × 0.0100 = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol in 1.00 L, so [H⁺] = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ and pH = 3.00. Dilution by a factor of 100 raises the pH by 2 units from 1.00.

questions.stem: Why is unpolluted rainwater slightly acidic, with a pH of about 5.6?
options: Nitrogen dissolves to form nitric acid, a strong acid, in the raindrops
Water molecules in the clouds lose their hydroxide ions to the air
Carbon dioxide dissolves to form carbonic acid, a weak acid that releases H⁺ ions
Oxygen dissolves to form an acid that releases H⁺ ions in the raindrops
questions.explanation: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ and H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. Carbonic acid is weak, so natural rain is only slightly acidic. Rain below pH 5.6 is caused by oxides of sulfur and nitrogen.

questions.stem: Which human activity is a major source of the sulfur dioxide that causes acid rain?
options: Burning natural gas in household heaters
Releasing refrigerant gases from old fridges
Burning coal that contains sulfur compounds
questions.explanation: Coal contains sulfur compounds that burn to SO₂, which forms H₂SO₃ and, after oxidation, H₂SO₄ in rain. Smelting sulfide ores is another major source.

questions.stem: Nitrogen dioxide from vehicle exhausts contributes to acid rain. Which is a balanced equation for its reaction with oxygen and water?
questions.explanation: Four HNO₃ contain 4 N, 4 H and 12 O. 4NO₂ provides 8 O, O₂ provides 2 and 2H₂O provides 2, totalling 12. The second equation has 7 O on the left and 6 on the right.

questions.stem: Which strategy removes sulfur dioxide from the waste gases of a coal-fired power station?
options: Building taller chimneys so the gases are released higher into the atmosphere
Passing the gases through water, which converts the SO₂ into harmless oxygen
Burning the coal at a higher temperature so the SO₂ breaks down to sulfur
Passing the gases through a slurry of lime or limestone, which reacts with the SO₂
questions.explanation: SO₂ is an acidic oxide, so it reacts with basic calcium compounds and is removed before release. Taller chimneys only spread the pollution further; they do not remove it.
